candidate_sources.title: Alternaria Leaf Spot of Brassicas | Cornell Vegetables
candidate_sources.snippet: Pin-sized black specks found on the leaf surface or stem enlarge concentrically, creating a distinct target spot or bull's eye lesion with a yellow halo. Symptoms are typically seen on older, lower leaves first. Alternaria brassicicola and A. brassicae infect cauliflower. Spores are produced after exposure to high relative humidity (~87%) and temperatures between 68-86°F.

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)-Alternaria Diseases | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Alternaria diseases of cauliflower and cabbage include black spot, gray leaf spot, and pod spot. Caused by Alternaria brassicicola, A. brassicae, and A. raphani. Lesions develop on leaves, petioles, stems, and cauliflower curds with a complete loss of marketability when heads are affected. Management includes sanitation, resistant varieties, and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria brassicae (dark spot of crucifers) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium entry for Alternaria brassicae, a major pathogen of Brassica crops including cauliflower. Comprehensive information on host range, disease symptoms, epidemiology, and management strategies for this economically important fungal disease affecting cruciferous vegetables.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria Leaf Spot of Cauliflower | Ohio Veggie Disease News
candidate_sources.snippet: Alternaria leaf spot of cauliflower caused by Alternaria brassicae is the most destructive disease at the curd stage and seed setting stage, attributed to causing 30-50% losses and in severe cases reaching up to 98% in seed crop. Disease management includes fungicides, cultural practices, and integrated approaches.

candidate_sources.title: Alternaria leaf spot and head rot of Brassica crops | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed guide on Alternaria leaf spot and head rot affecting Brassica crops including cauliflower. Covers identification of Alternaria brassicicola and A. brassicae, symptom development, environmental conditions favoring disease, and integrated management strategies including fungicide applications and cultural controls.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Soft Rot – Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Small, water-soaked areas appear and rapidly enlarge. Tissue becomes soft and mushy within days, and the affected plant part may collapse. Interior tissues become mushy and discolored, ranging from cream to black, with an offensive odor usually present. Caused by Pectobacterium carotovorum (formerly Erwinia carotovora).

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)-Bacterial Soft Rot Erwinia
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial soft rot of cabbage and cauliflower is caused by Erwinia carotovora subspecies. The disease causes water-soaked, sunken lesions that rapidly decay. The soft-rot bacterium enters through growth cracks or wounds caused by cold temperatures, insects, other disease organisms, or mechanical damage. Disease is most severe at 70-80°F with limited oxygen.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Soft Rot | USU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Soft rots are caused by several bacteria, most commonly Pectobacterium species (particularly Pectobacterium carotovorum) and Dickeya species (particularly Dickeya dadantii). Symptoms include water-soaked spots that enlarge and become sunken and soft. Rot can occur over a wide temperature range, with the worst decay between 70-80°F, particularly when oxygen is limited.

candidate_sources.title: Black Rot of Brassicas | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot causes yellow v-shaped lesions on leaves that extend toward the base, with distinct blackening of veins. The disease is caused by the seed-borne bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. As disease progresses, inner tissues blacken and water/nutrient flow is inhibited, leading to plant death.

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)—Black Rot | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot of cauliflower and cabbage presents as yellow v-shaped lesions that may show blackened veins. The pathogen, Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, is seed-borne and can persist in soil for 40-60 days and up to 2 years on infected debris. Particularly problematic in winter cauliflowers where wrapper leaves are lost.

candidate_sources.title: Brassicas, Black Rot | Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot on brassicas including cauliflower causes characteristic v-shaped yellow lesions extending from leaf margins toward the base. The disease is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris. Symptoms may not appear for more than a month after plant growth starts, making early detection difficult.

candidate_sources.title: Downy Mildew on Brassica Crops
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew on brassica crops including cauliflower is caused by the oomycete Hyaloperonospora parasitica. Symptoms on curds appear as pale brown to gray discoloration, with grayish or black spots on stems. On foliage, small angular yellow lesions develop on upper leaf surfaces, with gray-white spore masses on undersides. Infection occurs from airborne sporangia and systemic infections from oospores. Moderate temperatures (68-75°F) and high humidity favor disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Brassicas, Downy Mildew
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew of brassicas (including cauliflower) is caused by Hyaloperonospora parasitica. Yellow angular lesions form on upper leaf surfaces with characteristic gray-white powdery growth on undersides. On cauliflower heads, pale brown discoloration and darkening of interior tissues indicates systemic infection. The disease spreads via airborne spores and is favored by cool, moist conditions. Management includes resistant varieties, crop rotation, and fungicide applications when needed.

candidate_sources.title: Cabbage and Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea)—Downy Mildew (Staghead)
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew, also called staghead, is a disease of brassica crops including cauliflower caused by the oomycete pathogen Hyaloperonospora parasitica. Characteristic symptoms include downy growth (sporangia) on leaf undersides and systemic infections that discolor curds. The disease is managed through resistant variety selection, sanitation of plant debris, and fungicide treatments during susceptible growth stages.
